title: Section 1.0 Using Transforming Commands for Visualizations

source.author: Written for this study guide
source.grounding: help.splunk.com Splunk Enterprise 10.4, SPL Search Reference

questions.stem: A search returns one row per host, with a column for each distinct `status` value. Which search produces that table?

options.text: `... | chart count OVER host BY status`
options.explanation: The field after OVER is the row-split, so it becomes the first column and the X-axis. The field after BY is the column-split, so each distinct status becomes a column header. That is exactly the described shape.

options.text: `... | chart count OVER status BY host`
options.explanation: This transposes the table. status becomes the row-split and each host becomes a column, which is the mirror image of what was asked for.

options.text: `... | stats count BY host status`
options.explanation: With stats, every unique host and status combination is its own row and both fields stay as columns. You get three columns and many rows, not one row per host.

options.text: `... | timechart count BY host status`
options.explanation: timechart accepts only one field in its BY clause, so this is a syntax error. It would also split rows by _time rather than by host.

questions.overallExplanation: chart takes a row-split and a column-split. `chart count OVER host BY status` and `chart count BY host status` are the same search: the first field named is the row-split, the second is the column-split. Swapping the two fields transposes the result table.

guide.verdictNote: The chart page defines the BY clause as `BY <row-split> <column-split>` with the comma optional, which is why the OVER form and the two-field BY form are equivalent.

docs.title: chart command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: Syntax section: the row-split becomes the X-axis, the column-split becomes the series.

questions.stem: Why does `index=web | timechart count BY host, status` fail?

options.text: timechart accepts only one field in its BY clause.
options.explanation: _time is always timechart's row-split, so the single BY field is the column-split. There is no second slot to fill.

options.text: timechart requires an explicit `span` whenever a BY clause is used.
options.explanation: span is optional. Without it timechart chooses a span from the time range, capped by the bins option, which defaults to 100.

options.text: The comma is invalid; `BY host status` would work.
options.explanation: The comma is optional in a BY clause and is not the problem. Removing it still leaves two fields, which timechart cannot take.

options.text: count cannot be split by more than one field on any command.
options.explanation: chart splits count by two fields routinely, and stats accepts a whole field list. The restriction belongs to timechart, not to count.

questions.overallExplanation: Count fields, not clauses. Both chart and timechart have exactly one BY clause. chart's BY clause holds two fields because it needs a row-split and a column-split. timechart's holds one, because _time is already the row-split.

guide.verdictNote: The timechart syntax shows a single split-by-clause, in contrast to chart's `BY <row-split> <column-split>`.

docs.title: timechart command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: Syntax: _time is the implied row-split, leaving one split-by field.

questions.stem: In `chart` and `timechart`, which option controls the series that collects values excluded by `limit`, and what is that series called by default?

options.text: `useother`, and the series is labelled OTHER
options.explanation: useother controls the catch-all series for values the limit or where-clause excluded. Its label comes from otherstr, which defaults to OTHER, and useother defaults to true on both commands.

options.text: `usenull`, and the series is labelled NULL
options.explanation: usenull governs a different series entirely: events that have no value for the split-by field. Its label comes from nullstr, default NULL.

options.text: `useother`, and the series is labelled NULL
options.explanation: The option is right but the label is not. NULL is nullstr's default and belongs to the missing-field series, not the excluded-values series.

options.text: `otherstr`, and the series is labelled OTHER
options.explanation: otherstr only renames the series. Whether the series appears at all is controlled by useother.

questions.overallExplanation: Two separate series, two separate switches. usenull with nullstr covers events missing the split-by field. useother with otherstr covers values that were pushed out by limit. Both default to true on chart and timechart, and useother defaults to false on top.

guide.verdictNote: Worth carrying into the exam: the same option name defaults differently per command. useother is true on chart and timechart but false on top, which is why `top 5 host` shows no OTHER row.

docs.title: chart command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: Option table: usenull, nullstr, useother, otherstr and their defaults.

docs.title: top command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: useother default is false here, unlike on chart.

questions.stem: What does `limit=0` do on the `chart` command?

options.text: Returns all results, applying no series limit.
options.explanation: On chart, limit=0 removes the cap so every distinct value of the column-split gets a series.

options.text: Suppresses the series entirely, returning only the row-split column.
options.explanation: Nothing is suppressed. Zero means no limit here, not none.

options.text: Falls back to the default of the top ten values.
options.explanation: The top ten behaviour is what you get by omitting limit. Setting it to 0 explicitly overrides that default.

options.text: Errors, because limit must be a positive integer.
options.explanation: Zero is a documented value on chart, timechart, top and rare.

questions.overallExplanation: limit=0 means no limit across chart, timechart, top and rare. On top and rare it returns all values up to maxresultrows, whose default maximum is 50,000. Reading it as zero results is the trap.

guide.verdictNote: The related trap is what limit counts. On chart it limits the number of columns, not rows, and it is only valid when a column-split is specified.

questions.stem: Which two statements about the `chart` command are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: A statistical function is required; a bare field name is not valid.
options.explanation: The docs state you must specify a statistical function with chart. `chart sales BY product_name` fails; `chart sum(price) AS sales BY product_name` is the working form.

options.text: If both `span` and `bins` are given, `span` is used and `bins` is ignored.
options.explanation: This is documented behaviour on the bin options. Neither errors, and they do not compound.

options.text: The same field can be used both inside the function and as the split-by field.
options.explanation: It cannot. The documented workaround is to copy it first: `eval A1=A` then `chart sum(A) BY A1`.

options.text: `partial` and `fixedrange` are chart options that default to true.
options.explanation: Both exist only on timechart. cont exists on both commands and defaults to true on both.

questions.overallExplanation: Three chart facts worth separating from timechart: chart demands an aggregation, span wins over bins when both appear, and a field cannot be aggregated and split on at the same time. partial and fixedrange are timechart-only.

guide.verdictNote: Bin defaults differ by command and are worth memorising: chart defaults to bins=300, timechart to bins=100. Both are maximums, not targets.

docs.title: chart command (SPL Search Reference 10.4)
docs.note: Usage: a statistical function is required; bin options note that span takes precedence over bins.
